_content: Seismic Wave Propagation in Earth's Interior

Seismic wave propagation through Earth's crust and mantle follows the elastic wave equation, which describes how mechanical disturbances travel through solid and fluid media. Understanding these waves is fundamental to seismology, earthquake hazard assessment, and subsurface imaging for resource exploration.

P-waves (primary or compressional waves) are the fastest seismic waves, traveling through both solids and liquids. They compress and expand the material in the direction of wave travel, similar to sound waves in air. In typical crustal rocks, P-wave velocities range from 5 to 8 km/s, depending on composition and depth.

S-waves (secondary or shear waves) travel slower than P-waves and can only propagate through solids. They move material perpendicular to the direction of wave travel. The absence of S-waves in Earth's outer core provided the first evidence that this region is liquid.

Surface waves, including Rayleigh and Love waves, travel along Earth's surface and cause the most damage during earthquakes. Rayleigh waves produce a retrograde elliptical motion, while Love waves cause horizontal shearing. Their amplitudes decrease with depth, making them particularly sensitive to near-surface structure.

When seismic waves encounter boundaries between rock layers with different elastic properties, they undergo reflection, refraction, and mode conversion. Snell's law governs the angles of transmitted and reflected waves. At critical angles, head waves travel along interfaces, providing information about deep layer velocities.

Seismic attenuation, described by the quality factor Q, causes amplitude decay beyond geometric spreading. Intrinsic attenuation converts wave energy to heat through anelastic processes, while scattering attenuation redistributes energy due to small-scale heterogeneities. Both effects are frequency-dependent, with higher frequencies attenuating more rapidly.

Full waveform inversion (FWI) exploits the complete wavefield, including amplitudes and phases, to construct high-resolution subsurface models. This technique requires accurate forward modeling using numerical methods such as finite-difference or spectral-element methods, and iterative optimization to minimize the misfit between observed and synthetic seismograms.
Machine Learning Applications in Geophysics

Deep learning has transformed seismic data interpretation and geophysical modeling over the past decade. Traditional methods relied heavily on manual picking and rule-based algorithms, but modern neural network architectures can automatically extract features from raw seismic data with unprecedented accuracy.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for seismic facies classification and fault detection. By treating seismic sections as images, 2D and 3D CNNs can identify geological structures including faults, salt bodies, and stratigraphic horizons. U-Net architectures, originally developed for biomedical image segmentation, have been successfully adapted for seismic interpretation tasks.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, are applied to sequential seismic data analysis. They excel at tasks involving temporal patterns, such as seismic event detection, phase picking, and earthquake early warning systems.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) represent a paradigm shift by embedding physical constraints directly into the learning process. By incorporating the wave equation as a loss function penalty, PINNs can solve forward and inverse problems while respecting fundamental physics. This approach reduces the need for large labeled datasets and produces physically consistent results.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are used for seismic data augmentation and super-resolution. They can generate realistic synthetic seismograms for training when real data is scarce, and enhance the resolution of legacy surveys without reacquisition.

Transfer learning enables models trained on one geological setting to be adapted for another with limited local data. This is particularly valuable in exploration geophysics, where labeled data from new prospect areas is typically sparse. Pre-trained models from well-studied basins can be fine-tuned with small amounts of target domain data.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are emerging as powerful tools for modeling subsurface flow in porous media and analyzing seismic network data. They naturally handle irregular spatial structures and can capture complex spatial dependencies that regular grids cannot represent efficiently.
RiVault: AI-for-Science Platform on HPC Infrastructure

RiVault is an AI-for-Science platform designed to bring large language model (LLM) capabilities to high-performance computing environments. It provides on-demand LLM inference with the vLLM backend, proxied through LiteLLM for OpenAI API compatibility, enabling researchers to interact with AI models using familiar interfaces.

The platform architecture follows a security-first design. Models are pre-staged on the HPC filesystem, eliminating the need for runtime downloads. Network access is controlled through CoreDNS whitelisting and an EgressGuard proxy that monitors and filters outbound traffic. All communication between components traverses a private container network with no direct internet access from the inference engine.

UMRS (User Model Research System) provides the data management layer. It handles multi-modal data ingestion from S3-compatible storage, computes embeddings using configurable models (SentenceTransformers, CLIP, or remote vLLM endpoints), and stores vector representations in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. This enables semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over user datasets.

The orchestration system supports multiple backends. On HPC clusters, Slurm scheduling provisions compute nodes with GPU resources, launches containerized inference stacks, and establishes SSH tunnels for secure communication. A Kubernetes backend is also available for cloud-native deployments. The hybrid scheduler can translate Kubernetes manifests into Slurm job specifications for environments transitioning between paradigms.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers extend the LLM's capabilities with tool calling. Built-in MCP servers include time queries, image segmentation via SAM3, and custom user-defined tools. The MCPO gateway aggregates multiple MCP servers behind a single endpoint, and LiteLLM routes tool calls to the appropriate server transparently.

The RAG pipeline implements hybrid search combining BM25 keyword matching with pgvector semantic similarity, fused through reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). Query rewriting by the LLM generates focused sub-queries for improved retrieval. Cross-encoder reranking refines the final result set before context assembly, which manages token budgets and deduplicates overlapping chunks.

OpenWebUI provides an interactive chat interface for end users. It connects to LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible API, supporting multi-turn conversations, file uploads, and tool-augmented responses. Researchers can ask questions over their domain-specific datasets without writing code.
Numerical Methods in Computational Geodynamics

Finite element methods (FEM) and spectral element methods (SEM) are the workhorses of computational geodynamics. These techniques discretize the governing partial differential equations — including the wave equation, Stokes flow, and heat equation — into systems of algebraic equations that can be solved on modern computing architectures.

The finite element method partitions the computational domain into a mesh of elements (triangles, quadrilaterals, tetrahedra, or hexahedra). Within each element, the solution is approximated by polynomial basis functions. The weak formulation of the governing PDE ensures that the method handles complex geometries and heterogeneous material properties naturally. Higher-order elements (quadratic, cubic) improve accuracy at the cost of additional degrees of freedom.

Spectral element methods combine the geometric flexibility of finite elements with the exponential convergence of spectral methods. By using high-order Lagrange polynomials on Gauss-Lobatto-Legendre points, SEM achieves spectral accuracy while maintaining element-wise structure. This makes SEM particularly efficient for wave propagation problems, where high accuracy per wavelength is essential. The SPECFEM family of codes, widely used in seismology, employs SEM for global and regional earthquake simulations.

Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) concentrates computational resources in regions with high solution gradients, such as fault zones or phase boundaries. Octree-based AMR dynamically subdivides hexahedral elements, while h-adaptivity adjusts element sizes and p-adaptivity increases polynomial order locally. Balancing refinement criteria with load distribution across processors is a key challenge for parallel AMR.

Time-stepping schemes must balance accuracy with stability. Explicit methods like Runge-Kutta and leapfrog are simple to implement and parallelize but are subject to the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition, which limits the time step based on the smallest element and fastest wave speed. Implicit methods remove this restriction but require solving large linear systems at each step, making them computationally expensive for wave problems.

Preconditioning is essential for efficient iterative solvers. Multigrid methods, both geometric and algebraic (AMG), reduce iteration counts by addressing error components at multiple resolution levels. Domain decomposition preconditioners partition the problem across processors, with Schwarz-type methods exchanging boundary data. For indefinite systems arising from Stokes equations, block preconditioners that exploit the saddle-point structure are necessary.

Matrix-free implementations avoid assembling global stiffness matrices, computing matrix-vector products element-by-element instead. This approach reduces memory requirements from O(N^2) to O(N) and improves cache efficiency on modern architectures. Combined with sum factorization for tensor-product elements, matrix-free SEM can achieve near-peak hardware performance.
High-Performance Computing for Scientific Simulations

High-performance computing (HPC) enables large-scale scientific simulations that would be impossible on standard workstations. Modern supercomputers combine thousands of processors, massive memory systems, and high-bandwidth interconnects to solve computationally intensive problems in physics, chemistry, biology, and earth sciences.

GPU acceleration has revolutionized scientific computing. NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm provide programming frameworks for exploiting the massive parallelism of graphics processing units. A single modern GPU can deliver tens of teraflops of floating-point performance, making them ideal for matrix operations, finite-element solvers, and neural network training. The latest GPU architectures, including NVIDIA Blackwell and AMD Instinct, push the boundaries further with hardware support for mixed-precision arithmetic and specialized tensor cores.

The Slurm Workload Manager is the dominant job scheduler in HPC environments. It allocates compute resources, manages job queues with priority scheduling, and enforces fair-share policies among users. Slurm supports GPU-aware scheduling through GRES (Generic RESource) configuration, allowing jobs to request specific GPU types and quantities. Job arrays, dependencies, and preemption enable complex workflow orchestration.

Containerization ensures reproducibility in HPC. Singularity (now Apptainer) was designed specifically for multi-tenant HPC systems, running containers without requiring root privileges. Podman provides a Docker-compatible interface with rootless operation and better security isolation. Container images can encapsulate entire software stacks, including GPU drivers and scientific libraries, ensuring consistent execution across different clusters.

MPI (Message Passing Interface) remains the standard for distributed-memory parallel computing. Implementations such as OpenMPI and MPICH support collective communication patterns including broadcast, gather, scatter, and all-reduce operations. Modern MPI implementations leverage RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) over InfiniBand or RoCE networks for low-latency, high-bandwidth communication.

Parallel file systems like Lustre and GPFS provide the I/O bandwidth needed for large-scale simulations. Data-intensive applications such as seismic processing and climate modeling generate petabytes of output that must be written and read efficiently. Burst buffers and solid-state storage tiers help bridge the gap between compute speed and storage bandwidth.

Workflow management tools such as Nextflow, Snakemake, and Dask enable scientists to express complex computational pipelines that span multiple HPC jobs, handle data dependencies, and provide provenance tracking for reproducible research.
